rv.q: I'm so glad I saw Bluets. Without more story to sustain its 80 minutes, though, I was also so glad when it ended.
Ultimately, it’s a five-year-old Katie Mitchell show, that’s extremely cool to get to see but falls a bit oddly as the very first main house show of Byrne’s very first season.
My overriding feeling at the end of the 80 minutes was that Bluets is not a quarter as profound as Mitchell thinks it is.
Here, 80 minutes begins to feel like eight hours.
The story enfolds incredibly before our eyes, the urban scenes the perfect environment for such loneliness.
Bluets proves challenging and thus makes a good start as the first main house production of David Byrne’s leadership as Artistic Director at the Royal Court.
It’s a fascinating start to a new era in the larger Royal Court space.
This is not a safe production; it is rebellious, challenging
Unfortunately, it’s neither as adventurous nor as edgy as it claims to be.
Not everyone will love the experimental nature of Bluets, but those who embrace its unconventional approach will be richly rewarded.

My own thoughts are that, clever though the choreography is, generating a visual illusion in front of our eyes, the prop manoeuvres by semi visible stage crew are off putting, interrupting the visual presentation, often unnecessarily.
Here, any attempts to foster our compassion are overshadowed by an ambition to woo us with style.

cn.t: Mitchell's tech-heavy "live cinema" adaptation of Nelson's meditation on blue and heartbreak dazzles visually but divides critics—some find it poetically innovative, others see repetitive melancholia that wastes its starry cast.
